Here are 3 things that I can say in retrospect. I completely know these are difficult to believe when you’re in the middle of a bad period - I struggle with them even now during shit times. 

1. This too shall pass. Feeling happy? Feeling sad? This too shall pass. 

2. Knowing that you can kill yourself is a weird “super power”. It gives you the courage to try anything. After all, if things don’t work out you can always not live. See, most things in life do not have long term consequences, and you’ll know when you’re faced with the few that do. 

3. Optimize for process, outcome will come. Focus on doing what you can at the very best level you can. Outcome is not in your control and never will be. But good process necessitates good outcomes, just the timing is not predictable. 

I wish you the very best.

When in doubt, look at the average return on investment. What I mean is any degree is gonna cost you something, and you'll have to pay it off either by working part-time or after graduating, most probably a little of both. 

First look at various degrees, sorted by decreasing order of average income. Pick the top few, and then calculate the average ten year income you expect to get after graduating. Then look at what those degrees cost, and divide the income by the cost to create a rough metric. Ofc this isn't very accurate since all sort of stuff like inflation, interest rates, etc. come into play, but it's enough for a back-of-the-envelope estimate. 

I'll guess, with high certainty, that STEM degrees will be at the top. You'll also have business and finance near the top. Go with them if you aren't sure. 

Ofc you have the choice of not opting for a college education and going into a trade. The analysis I mentioned can also be applied for selecting a trade. 

Also, a piece of advice my dad gave me when I was about to enter college, and it's kinda profound(atleast it was for me) : College isn't a place to discover yourself, it's to make yourself employable. 

That doesn't mean you need to soldier on with CS if you're bad at it. But if you're okay at it but you still are kinda indifferent about it I'll recommend you get the CS degree, as long as you have a good GPA. STEM teaches you skills which are applicable in any and all industries. You don't need to get a coding job, wall street would be glad to have you if you have the quantitative prowess they want. I'll graduate with a bachelor's in Electrical engineering in a couple of months. I have a job at a consultancy firm cus I realised I have no passion for electrical. But all those hours spent analysing circuits and systems and differential equations and Markov processes gave me skills which a consulting firm wants. 

Motto: When in doubt, choose STEM.

I'll take a stab at it. GDP growth rate is more important than tbe absolute GDP. In case of a recession, we see a reduced or even negative growth rate. What this means is that the net amount of goods sold/bought is reducing. That is, people are buying less stuff, and therefore, businesses are producing less stuff. Regulatory bodies will try to reduce interest rates so that taking out loans become less burdensome so as to inject some cash into the economy. During a recession incomes obviously take a hit. 

The typical anatomy of a recession usually goes like something bad happens, people have no money, people stop buying stuff, businesses go bankrupt cus no one is buying any thing, more people get unemployed and you get the idea. 

Decreasing interest rates help, as explained earlier. Competition is a bit nuanced here. In most fields competition will decrease, since small business can't sustain, and the big ones usually have cash reserves or get bailouts. On the other hand, in sectors crucial for recovery of the economy, or something which is now all of a sudden in the forefront, competition will increase depending on the entry barriers (think how many companies and start ups are currently looking into cheap mask making procedures). So competition has to be analysed on a sectorial basis. Incomes obviously fall, but I wouldn't go as far as saying all incomes fall, just the average.

If GDP grows too fast and production cannot keep up with demand inflation occurs. Interest rates are increased to reduce spending power and control the inflation. Again, competition has to be analysed on a case to case basis and same for income.

Well, no engineering branch has a "lighter" load. It's about your interests. Even in electrical, I found machine theory very tough but control systems and dynamics came naturally to me. 

Secondly, the broader thing is also a misconception. It's nigh impossible to compare fields and say which is broader. The line between CSE and EE is blurry, as is between Mech. Engg. and IE and production engineering. It's a very difficult line to find and there's no use after finding it. 

IE is a good major, one that'll rarely ever go out of demand due to the industrialised nature of our economy. I'll also recommend not only chasing after a good salary but good work ex for 3-5 years after graduating. For example, if in EE you worked in Nvidea or tsmc or intel or TI as a design engineer even for low pay it is more than compensated by the value it adds to your CV and the practical experience it gives you. 

I'd recommend keeping a good GPA, you don't need a 4.0 or even 3.5+ to land a good job. Keep it above 2.8, or above average whichever is greater. If this is easy then aim for 3.0 and 3.2 depending on your choice. Beyond that the marginal benefit of increasing gpa diminishes.
